757.title: "If he said it, it is true"
757.hook: Mecca mocks the night journey, and Abu Bakr says, if he said it, it is true (sirah)
757.carry: he weighed the speaker, not the distance
757.howItsDone: Muslims remember Abu Bakr by the title al-Siddiq and retell his answer when they recall the night journey, often on the night of al-Isra wal-Mi'raj.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Musa, and fifty become five. Your line was: five, weighing fifty.

Morning in Mecca. The Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, tells the people what happened in the night: he was carried to Jerusalem and brought back before dawn. In the sirah the reaction is fast. Some laugh. Ibn Ishaq reports that some who had believed turned back. A caravan takes a month to get there and a month to return, people say, and he did it in one night? A few of them hurry off to find his close friend, Abu Bakr. Have you heard what your companion is saying now? Today: al-Siddiq.
screen: `CARRIED BY NIGHT.` → `MECCA LAUGHS.` → `THEY RUN TO ABU BAKR.`

segments.voice: Abu Bakr asks one question first: did he say that? Yes, they say. In Ibn Ishaq's account he answers: if he said it, then it is true. And he adds, roughly: why are you so surprised? He tells me news comes to him from heaven, from God, in an hour of the night or the day, and I believe him in that. This is further than Jerusalem. Then Abu Bakr goes to the Prophet and asks him to describe the city, and as he does, Abu Bakr keeps saying: you have spoken the truth. Tradition says this is the day he was called al-Siddiq, the one who affirms the truth. Bukhari has a report from the Prophet's side of that morning: when Quraysh would not believe him, Allah showed him Jerusalem, and he described it to them while looking at it. Notice what Abu Bakr's trust rests on. Not a feeling about miracles, but long knowledge of one man, and of what he has said before. He doesn't weigh the distance to Jerusalem. He weighs the speaker. And with his answer, this part of the story, sorrow, Ta'if and the night journey, comes to its close. It began with two graves, Khadijah's and Abu Talib's. It closes with a friend who stays when others mock.

Let their face settle in front of you, and notice how much of your life rests, quietly, on people like this. If you pray, you can thank God for that person by name.
Al-Siddiq, the one who affirms the truth. Abu Bakr's title, earned when he trusted the Prophet's word about the night journey without arguing the distance. Today's word.
Your line: he weighed the speaker, not the distance. Trust like that is built long before it's needed. See you tomorrow.

758.title: Six men from Yathrib
758.hook: at the pilgrimage six men from Yathrib listen and believe
758.howItsDone: Muslims retell the meeting with the six men of Yathrib as the start of the road to Medina, the turning point after the hardest years in Mecca.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Abu Bakr's answer, al-Siddiq. Your line was: he weighed the speaker, not the distance.
screen: `HE WEIGHED THE SPEAKER, NOT THE DISTANCE.`

segments.voice: Pilgrimage season. Tents and travelers fill the valleys around Mecca, tribes come from far away, and Ibn Ishaq says the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, made a habit of these crowds: camp to camp, introducing himself, asking who would hear him out. Mostly they turned away. After Ta'if, after the mocking, he keeps going. Then one evening, near a place called Aqaba, he meets a small group from a town to the north. Ibn Ishaq counts them: six men from Yathrib. He asks them a simple question. Will you sit with me, and let me speak to you? Today: Yathrib.
screen: `CAMP AFTER CAMP.` → `MOSTLY TURNED AWAY.` → `WILL YOU SIT WITH ME?`

segments.voice: They sit. He tells them about God and recites the Qur'an. And something, Ibn Ishaq says, had already prepared them. In Yathrib they lived beside Jewish neighbors, people of scripture, who had spoken of a prophet who would come. So the six look at each other: this may be the prophet they told us about. Let's not be the last to answer him. And they believe. They tell him about home, too. Yathrib was worn down by feuding between its own clans: we have left our people, and no people are so divided by enmity as they are. Perhaps God will unite them through you. We'll go home and call them to this, and if God gathers them around you, no man will be stronger than you. Then they go home and talk. Before long, Ibn Ishaq says, there was hardly a house in Yathrib where the Prophet wasn't spoken of. Look at the shape of it. Years of closed doors in Mecca. A walk to Ta'if that ended in stones. Then six strangers, from a town he has never lived in, who simply listen. Nobody argues them into it. They sit, they hear, they take it home. A new part of the story begins: toward Yathrib, the town that will one day be called Medina, the city.
screen: `THEY SIT, AND HE RECITES.` · `THIS MAY BE THE PROPHET.` · `A TOWN WORN DOWN BY FEUDS.` · `THEY TAKE IT HOME.` · then, large: `SIX LISTENED.`

segments.voice: Think of a stranger you're likely to meet soon: someone at a counter, a new person at work, a neighbor you've only nodded to. Picture letting them finish, not planning your reply, not checking the time, just hearing what they have to say. If you pray, you can ask God for an open ear.
Yathrib. The town, later called Medina, whose six strangers sat, listened to the Prophet at the pilgrimage, believed, and carried the news home. Today's word.
Your line: six listened. Big turns can start that small. Day seven hundred fifty-eight, done.

759.title: The first pledge of Aqaba
759.hook: twelve pledge not to steal, lie, kill their children or slander
759.howItsDone: Muslims remember the first pledge of Aqaba as a promise about how to live, and the same list of conduct appears in the Qur'an's description of women pledging to the Prophet.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Yathrib, and six strangers who sat and heard him. Your line was: six listened.

A year goes by. The pilgrimage comes round again, and so do the men from Yathrib: twelve of them this time, Ibn Ishaq says. They meet the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, at the same spot, Aqaba, a narrow pass on the edge of Mina, away from the crowds. They've had a year at home to talk, to argue, to wonder. Now they've come back with their hands out. Not to ask for anything. To give their word. Today: the first pledge of Aqaba.
screen: `A YEAR LATER.` → `TWELVE COME BACK.` → `HANDS OUT TO PLEDGE.`

segments.voice: What did they promise? Ubada ibn al-Samit, whom the sirah names among the twelve, gives the terms in Sahih al-Bukhari. The Prophet said: pledge to me that you will not set up any partner with God, that you will not steal, that you will not commit adultery, that you will not kill your children, that you will not bring a slander you have invented between your hands and feet, and that you will not disobey me in what is right. Whoever keeps it, his reward is with God. Look at that list. No army, no money, no promise to fight for anyone. It's about how they will live: their hands, their tongues, their homes, their children. Ibn Ishaq says this kind of pledge came to be called the pledge of women, and that it carried no promise of war. The Qur'an, in surah sixty, describes believing women pledging much the same things to the Prophet. And there's a mercy built in. In Ubada's report the Prophet adds: whoever falls into any of these and is punished in this world, that is an expiation. And whoever falls and God covers it, it is up to God, to forgive or to punish. The pledge is clear, and realistic. It expects people to be tested, and it doesn't throw them away when they stumble. The twelve go home carrying a promise about conduct. Not yet a promise of protection. That comes later.

Aqaba, the narrow pass where twelve men of Yathrib pledged the Prophet a way of living, not a war. Today's word.
Your line: a pledge of conduct. Clear enough to keep, with room for anyone who stumbles. Until tomorrow.

760.title: Mus'ab the teacher
760.hook: Mus'ab ibn Umayr is sent to teach the Qur'an in Yathrib, and many believe
760.howItsDone: Muslims remember Mus'ab ibn Umayr as the teacher sent to Yathrib before the hijra, and his invitation to sit and listen is often retold when people talk about how to share the faith gently.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the first pledge at Aqaba. Your line was: a pledge of conduct.

The twelve are heading home with a promise and a problem. They believe, but who will teach them? Who will recite the Qur'an to their families, lead their prayer, answer the questions that come up at dinner? So the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, sends someone with them. Not a clan elder. Mus'ab ibn Umayr, a Meccan who, tradition says, had left a comfortable life behind for this faith. In Yathrib, Ibn Ishaq says, people came to call him simply the reciter. Today: al-Muqri.
screen: `WHO WILL TEACH THEM?` → `MUS'AB IS SENT.` → `THEY CALL HIM THE RECITER.`

segments.voice: Mus'ab stays with a man of Yathrib, As'ad ibn Zurara, and the two go out into the gardens and neighborhoods, reciting. Not everyone is pleased. One day, Ibn Ishaq says, a clan leader, Usayd ibn Hudayr, comes striding toward them with his spear, angry. What have you come here for, to make fools of our weak ones? Leave us, if you value your life. Mus'ab doesn't argue. He says, roughly: will you not sit down and listen? If you like what you hear, accept it. If you dislike it, we'll keep away from what you dislike. Usayd thinks that's fair. He plants his spear in the ground and sits. Mus'ab recites, and the story says that before Usayd had spoken a word, they could see the change in his face. He asks what a person does to enter this faith. Then Usayd sends a greater leader, Sa'd ibn Mu'adh, who comes in just as angry, and the same thing happens: an invitation to sit, a recitation, a changed face. Sa'd goes back to his own clan, Ibn Ishaq says, and asks how they regard him. When they answer with respect, he tells them he won't speak to them until they believe. Tradition says that by evening, his clan had. That's the whole method in the story: sit down, listen, you are free to say no. The teacher puts the words in front of people, and steps back.

761.title: The second pledge
761.hook: seventy-three men and two women pledge to protect him as their own
761.howItsDone: Muslims remember the second pledge of Aqaba as the promise that opened the way to Medina, and honor the Ansar, the helpers of Medina, for keeping it.

segments.voice: Yesterday: al-Muqri, Mus'ab the reciter in Yathrib. Your line was: the first teacher.

Another pilgrimage. Another night at Aqaba. But this time it's after dark, a third of the night gone, and people are slipping away from their sleeping companions one or two at a time, creeping like birds, Ibn Ishaq says. They gather in a ravine: seventy-three men and two women, by his count. One of the women is Nusayba bint Ka'b, known as Umm Umara. They've come to make a different kind of promise than the twelve made a year before. Today: Aqaba.
screen: `AFTER DARK, IN A RAVINE.` → `SLIPPING AWAY ONE BY ONE.` → `SEVENTY-THREE MEN, TWO WOMEN.`

segments.voice: The Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, comes with his uncle al-Abbas, who, Ibn Ishaq says, still followed the religion of his people but came to look after his nephew. Al-Abbas speaks first, and bluntly. He is safe among his own clan. If you're going to take him, be sure you can protect him. If not, leave him now. The Prophet recites the Qur'an to them and asks for their pledge: that they protect him as they protect their own women and children. Al-Bara ibn Ma'rur takes his hand and says yes: we are people of war and weapons. Then Abu al-Haytham raises a hard question. We have ties with other people in Yathrib, and we'll be cutting them. If we do this, and God gives you victory, will you go back to your own people and leave us? The story says the Prophet smiled and answered: no. Blood is blood. I am of you and you are of me. I will fight whom you fight, and make peace with whom you make peace. See what's changed. The first pledge was about conduct. This one is about bodies and homes: we will stand in front of you. And it runs both ways; they ask for his loyalty as clearly as he asks for theirs. Their reward, he tells them, is paradise. In the story, no wealth is promised, and no power. Only that.

762.title: Slipping out
762.hook: Muslims leave Mecca quietly, in small groups, leaving homes and property
762.howItsDone: Muslims call those who left Mecca for Medina the Muhajirun, the emigrants, and retell stories like Umm Salama's and Suhayb's to honor what the hijra cost them.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the second pledge at Aqaba. Your line was: protect him as your own.

A door closes in Mecca before dawn, and the family behind it isn't coming back. With the pledge made, the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, tells his followers they can go: God has given them brothers in Yathrib and a home to go to. So they go. Not all together. In ones and twos and families, quietly, so Quraysh won't stop them. Houses are left standing behind them. Today: slipping out.
screen: `A DOOR CLOSES BEFORE DAWN.` → `IN ONES AND TWOS.` → `HOUSES LEFT STANDING.`

segments.voice: Ibn Ishaq keeps some of these departures in close-up. One is Umm Salama's. She sets out with her husband, Abu Salama, and their little son. Her own clan stops them and takes her back: you can go, they tell him, but not with our daughter. Then his clan arrives, furious, and takes the child: if you've kept her, we keep our boy. In a single stop on the road, a family is pulled into three pieces. Abu Salama goes on to Yathrib alone. Umm Salama, in her own telling, goes out every morning to the place where it happened and weeps until evening, for a long time, until a relative takes pity and persuades the clans to let her go. She gets her son back and sets out alone, on a camel, with the boy in her lap. Another is Suhayb, called the Roman, who had come to Mecca with nothing and done well in trade. As he leaves, the story goes, men of Quraysh block him: you came here poor and grew rich among us, and now you'll leave with it all? He asks: if I give you my wealth, will you let me pass? They say yes, and he hands it over. When the Prophet hears, tradition says he answered: Suhayb has made a profitable trade. That's what slipping out looked like. Not a march. A long series of private losses: a house, savings, a morning by the road. The Qur'an speaks of those who emigrated and were driven from their homes and their wealth. These are some of their faces.

763.title: The plot
763.hook: the Meccan leaders plan to kill him with a man from every clan
763.howItsDone: Muslims recite the verse about this plot (8:30) and retell the night of the council when they remember the hijra, often as a reminder to trust God's planning over their own.

segments.voice: Yesterday: slipping out, the believers leaving Mecca. Your line was: they left everything.

Mecca is emptying out. House after house of believers stands locked, the owners gone north to Yathrib, where they now have protectors. The leaders of Quraysh can see where this is heading. The Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, is still in the city, with Abu Bakr and Ali. If he joins the others, he'll be out of reach, among people sworn to defend him. So they meet in the council house, the Dar al-Nadwa. One question on the table: what do we do about him? Today: the plot.
screen: `MECCA EMPTYING OUT.` → `THE COUNCIL HOUSE.` → `WHAT DO WE DO ABOUT HIM?`

segments.voice: Ibn Ishaq records the debate. One voice says: lock him up in irons and wait for him to die, as poets have died before. No, says another: his followers will hear and come to free him. Drive him out, then, and we'll be rid of him. No: look how sweet his speech is, how he wins hearts. He'll gather an army and come back. Then Abu Jahl gives the plan they choose. Take one strong young man from every clan, give each a sharp sword, and let them strike him all at once, like a single man. His blood will be spread across all the clans, his family can't fight everyone, and they'll have to take blood money instead. It's a cold plan, and clever: everyone's crime, so no one's. Ibn Ishaq adds a strange detail. The voice that knocked down prison and exile, and praised the killing, belonged to an old man from Najd who had joined the meeting, and Ibn Ishaq says he was Iblis, Satan, in disguise. What the Qur'an says about that night is short. It reminds the Prophet of when those who disbelieved plotted against him, to hold him captive, or kill him, or drive him out. They plotted, and God plotted, and God is the best of planners. In the common reading, the verse lists the same three options the council argued over: captivity, killing, exile. And it doesn't describe a counter-army. It just sets their planning beside God's.
screen: `LOCK HIM UP, OR DRIVE HIM OUT?` · `A YOUNG MAN FROM EVERY CLAN.` · `EVERYONE'S CRIME, NO ONE'S.` · `THEY PLOTTED, AND GOD PLOTTED.` · then, large: `THEY PLANNED; ALLAH PLANNED.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind something you're anxious about: a decision others are making about you, a meeting, a diagnosis, a person who seems set against you, and notice how much of the planning is out of your hands. Then remember that the story doesn't end with the council's vote. If you pray, you can ask God for protection in your own words, or with a line you know from the Qur'an; if you don't, simply breathe out the part you can't control.
